result:
The first thing that comes is the low hum of the ceiling fan in a rented room in Lisbon at 3:17 a.m. I’m not there, but I can hear it anyway. That sound has followed me for years, the same way certain memories do: not because they’re important, but because they refuse to resolve. The fan never quite synced with anything. It just kept turning, dragging warm air across my face like an indifferent hand.

I think about how most of us are walking around carrying small, private museums. Not the grand ones with marble floors. More like shoeboxes under the bed filled with ticket stubs, cracked phone screens, the smell of someone’s neck from 2009. We open them alone. We close them quickly. The older I get the more I realize the exhibits aren’t even about the events themselves. They’re about who I was when I thought those events were permanent.

There’s a Japanese concept I keep returning to lately: *mono no aware*. The gentle sadness at the transience of things. Not depression. Not even nostalgia exactly. Just this soft, almost courteous acknowledgment that the cherry blossoms are already falling while you’re still trying to take their picture. I like that it doesn’t ask you to fix anything. It only asks you to notice.

I’ve been trying to notice more.

Like how light moves across a wooden table in the morning depending on what city you’re in. In Reykjavik it’s thin and metallic. In Oaxaca it’s thick and golden, like someone poured mescal into the air. Same sun, different stories. The table doesn’t care. It just holds whatever we put on it—coffee, passports, unsent apologies—and keeps being a table.

Sometimes I imagine all the versions of myself that didn’t happen. The one who stayed in the band. The one who said yes to the girl in Lisbon. The one who never started writing in the first place and became, I don’t know, a decent welder. They’re not ghosts. They’re more like roads I can still see in the rearview mirror, getting smaller. I don’t mourn them anymore. I just wave.

There’s this thing my grandmother used to say when she was losing her memory: “The light is the same, only the lamps are different.” She said it with complete conviction even when she couldn’t remember my name. I think she was trying to tell me that consciousness is continuous, but the containers we pour it into keep changing shape. Some days I’m a cracked mug. Some days I’m a cathedral. The light doesn’t mind.

I’ve been reading physics again, the way other people read poetry. Not because I understand the math (I don’t), but because the metaphors keep sneaking up on me and breaking my heart. Entanglement. How two particles can be so far apart that not even light could travel between them in the age of the universe, yet if you tickle one the other laughs instantly. The universe is apparently full of these ridiculous love stories that violate every reasonable notion of distance. I find that comforting in a way I can’t quite explain.

Maybe we’re all a little entangled.

I keep a small rock in my pocket that I picked up on a beach in Cornwall in 2017. It’s nothing special. Grey. Slightly heart-shaped if you squint. I’ve carried it through eight countries and two breakups. Every time I touch it I remember how cold the water was and how the wind tried to take my hat and how completely alive I felt for no particular reason. The rock costs me nothing and gives me everything. That seems like a good trade.

There’s a line from a poem I can’t remember properly that goes something like “We are all just trying to get back to the sea.” I like that image. All of us rivers of varying degrees of cleanliness and violence, cutting through whatever landscape life gave us, trying to remember what we were before we became individuals. Before names. Before shame. Before we learned how to disappoint people.

I disappoint people less now. Not because I’m better. Just because I disappoint myself more honestly.

The fan is still turning somewhere. I can hear it between these words. Maybe it’s not in Lisbon anymore. Maybe it followed me. Or maybe I’m the one who’s been turning this whole time and the room was only ever an idea.

There are 312 words left in my allowance and I want to use them to say something useful but all I can think is this:

Be kind to the person you were at 2 a.m. last Tuesday when everything felt like evidence against you. They were doing their best with the light they had. The lamps change. The light stays the same. Carry your stupid little rock. Wave at the roads not taken. Notice the way morning arrives differently in every city and let that be enough.

The fan slows down. Or maybe I do.

Either way, here we are. Still turning. Still listening for the sea.
